title: United Arab Emirates
subtitle: 1971–today · Federation, Oil Wealth, Dubai's Reinvention and an Assertive Foreign Policy

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: An Abu Dhabi presidency and a Dubai premiership over a federation of seven emirates

entries.label: Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan — founding President
entries.hint: Zayed, Ruler of Abu Dhabi, was the driving force behind the 1971 federation and its President for 33 years, using Abu Dhabi's oil revenue to bind the emirates together with federal spending. His consensus style and pan-Arab aid diplomacy set the state's early character.
entries.note: UAE Constitution (1971, provisional; permanent 1996); Heard-Bey, 'From Trucial States to United Arab Emirates' (1982); WAM (state news agency) obituary coverage, 2004.

entries.label: Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan
entries.hint: Khalifa succeeded his father as Ruler of Abu Dhabi and President. His tenure covered the 2008–09 Dubai debt crisis — resolved by an Abu Dhabi bailout after which the world's tallest tower was renamed Burj Khalifa — and, after a 2014 stroke, a long period in which his half-brother Mohamed exercised day-to-day authority.
entries.note: Federal Supreme Council election, November 2004; the January 2014 announcement of his stroke; state media, 2014–2022.

entries.label: Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan
entries.hint: Elected President the day after Khalifa's death in May 2022, Mohamed bin Zayed had already shaped a decade of UAE policy as crown prince — the military build-up, the interventions in Yemen and Libya, the 2020 normalisation with Israel. As of 2025 he also chairs the reorganised presidential court and the sovereign wealth apparatus.
entries.note: Federal Supreme Council election, 14 May 2022; constitutional amendment creating a Vice-President role for Mansour bin Zayed alongside Mohammed bin Rashid, 2023. Tenure ongoing as of 2025.

entries.label: Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum — builder of Dubai
entries.hint: Ruler of Dubai and the federation's Vice-President from 1971 and Prime Minister from 1979, Rashid drove Dubai's infrastructure gamble — Port Rashid, the Jebel Ali port and free zone, the dry dock, the airport — laying the base for a trade economy independent of the emirate's modest oil.
entries.note: Federal government records; the premiership passed to Rashid in 1979 (from Maktoum bin Rashid, who resumed it 1990–2006). Davidson, 'Dubai: The Vulnerability of Success' (2008).

entries.label: Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum
entries.hint: Ruler of Dubai, and the UAE's Vice-President and Prime Minister since 2006, Mohammed bin Rashid oversaw Dubai's post-2009 recovery, the Expo 2020 bid, and a stream of federal 'vision' plans. A 2020 UK High Court fact-finding judgment made adverse findings against him in the case of his daughters Latifa and Shamsa and his former wife.
entries.note: assumed the premiership on Maktoum bin Rashid's death, January 2006; England and Wales High Court, 'Al Maktoum v Al Hussein' fact-finding judgment, March 2020 (published).

entries.label: The Supreme Council and the temporary constitution made permanent
entries.hint: The seven rulers form the Supreme Council, which elects the President and Vice-President and holds ultimate authority; Ras al-Khaimah joined in February 1972. The 1971 constitution was renewed every five years as 'provisional' until made permanent in 1996, with Abu Dhabi confirmed as the capital.
entries.note: UAE Constitution, Articles on the Supreme Council; the 1996 constitutional amendment; Peck, 'The United Arab Emirates: A Venture in Unity' (1986).

entries.label: The Federal National Council and the limits of participation
entries.hint: The 40-member FNC is a consultative body with no legislative veto. From 2006 half its members have been chosen by an appointed electoral college that has grown over time; the 2019 elections returned a chamber that is 50% women. Political parties remain banned.
entries.note: FNC electoral decrees (2006, 2011, 2015, 2019); the 2019 gender-parity directive; Freedom House country reports.

entries.label: Succession disputes within the emirates
entries.hint: The federation has absorbed internal crises: a 1987 coup attempt against Sultan al-Qasimi of Sharjah was reversed by the Supreme Council within days, and a contested Ras al-Khaimah succession in 2010 was settled in favour of Saud bin Saqr. The Council, not the street, adjudicates emirate power.
entries.note: the June 1987 Sharjah coup attempt and its reversal; the 2010 RAK succession; contemporaneous reporting and Davidson, 'The United Arab Emirates: A Study in Survival' (2005).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: From the seized islands to Yemen, Libya and drones over Abu Dhabi

entries.label: The islands and the Saudi border
entries.loc: Abu Musa, the Tunbs; the Shaybah frontier
entries.hint: The UAE inherited Ras al-Khaimah's and Sharjah's claim to the three islands Iran took in 1971 and pursues it diplomatically. Its land border with Saudi Arabia, fixed in the disputed 1974 Treaty of Jeddah, remained a source of quiet friction into the 2000s.
entries.note: the UAE's standing claim to Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa; the 1974 Treaty of Jeddah (text never fully published); Schofield, 'Territorial Foundations of the Gulf States' (1994).

entries.label: The Gulf War and the US security guarantee
entries.hint: Iraq's annexation of Kuwait showed how fast a Gulf state could vanish. The UAE joined the coalition, hosted coalition aircraft, and afterward signed a defence cooperation agreement with the United States (1994) that has anchored its security ever since.
entries.note: the 1991 Gulf War coalition; the 1994 US–UAE Defence Cooperation Agreement (its text classified); Al Dhafra Air Base host arrangements.

entries.label: Afghanistan deployment
entries.hint: The UAE sent special forces and a provincial reconstruction presence to Afghanistan under ISAF — the only Arab country to commit combat troops. The deployment deepened military ties with the US and NATO and gave the Emirati forces their first sustained expeditionary experience.
entries.note: UAE participation in ISAF (2003–2014); US and NATO acknowledgements; Roberts, 'Qatar and the UAE' comparative studies.

entries.label: The Yemen war
entries.loc: Aden, the south Yemen coast, Socotra
entries.hint: The UAE was the lead ground partner in the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, retaking Aden in 2015 and building up southern Yemeni forces, above all the Southern Transitional Council. It drew down its own troops from 2019 while keeping influence on the coast and islands.
entries.note: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reports (2016–2020); the 2019 UAE drawdown announcement; the UAE–STC relationship.

entries.label: Libya and the shadow wars
entries.hint: UN experts documented repeated UAE arms transfers and air strikes in support of Khalifa Haftar's forces in Libya, in breach of the arms embargo. The UAE also backed the 2013 change of government in Egypt and, later, was named in connection with support to a warring party in Sudan.
entries.note: UN Panel of Experts on Libya reports (2017–2021) documenting embargo violations; UN reporting on Sudan, 2024. The UAE denies the allegations.

entries.label: Houthi strikes on Abu Dhabi
entries.hint: Houthi drones and missiles struck fuel trucks near Abu Dhabi's airport and industrial area, killing three foreign workers — the first deadly attack on the UAE capital. US Patriot and Emirati THAAD batteries intercepted follow-on salvoes; the UAE re-engaged militarily in Yemen briefly afterward.
entries.note: the 17 and 24 January 2022 attacks; UAE Ministry of Interior statements; US CENTsentCOM confirmation of THAAD's first combat use.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A federal-emirate division of powers, common-law enclaves and a decade of legal reform

entries.label: The federal bargain — what is federal and what is not
entries.hint: Defence, foreign affairs, immigration, currency and federal justice are federal; oil and gas, land, natural resources and much policing stay with each emirate. Abu Dhabi and Dubai contribute most of the federal budget and hold effective veto power in the Supreme Council.
entries.note: UAE Constitution, Articles 120–121 (federal competences) and 122–123 (residual emirate powers).

entries.label: The 2020–2024 personal-status and penal reforms
entries.hint: A wave of decree-laws decriminalised alcohol consumption and unmarried cohabitation, ended reduced sentences for so-called honour killings, allowed non-Muslim residents a civil family law in Abu Dhabi, and recast parts of the penal and labour codes. Same-sex relations remained criminalised.
entries.note: Federal Decree-Laws of November 2020 and 2021–22; Abu Dhabi Law No. 14 of 2021 on civil personal status for non-Muslims; published in the Official Gazette.

entries.label: Common-law enclaves — the DIFC and ADGM
entries.hint: The Dubai International Financial Centre (2004) and Abu Dhabi Global Market (2015) are financial free zones with their own English-language, common-law courts and regulators, carved out of the UAE's civil-law system to reassure international finance.
entries.note: DIFC Law No. 3 of 2004; ADGM founding legislation (Federal Decree No. 15 of 2013; Abu Dhabi Law No. 4 of 2013). The DIFC Courts apply a common-law framework.

entries.label: Reforming the sponsorship (kafala) system
entries.hint: The Wages Protection System (2009) required salaries paid through banks; a 2017 law extended labour protections to domestic workers; the 2021 labour law and residency reforms loosened the tie between a visa and a single employer and introduced long-term 'golden' and 'green' visas.
entries.note: MOHRE Wages Protection System (2009); Federal Law No. 10 of 2017 (domestic workers); Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 (labour relations); ILO and Human Rights Watch assessments of the remaining gaps.

entries.label: Speech, association and the security laws
entries.hint: Cybercrime (2012, revised 2021), counter-terrorism (2014) and related laws criminalise a wide range of speech, protest and unlicensed association. The 2013 mass trial of 94 defendants (the 'UAE94') and the continued imprisonment of the activist Ahmed Mansoor since 2017 are the cases most cited by rights monitors.
entries.note: Federal Decree-Laws No. 5 of 2012 and No. 34 of 2021 (cybercrime); Law No. 7 of 2014 (counter-terrorism); UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention opinions on the UAE94 and on Ahmed Mansoor.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: State-managed Islam, the ban on political Islam, and interfaith building as policy

entries.label: Official Islam and the Grand Mosque
entries.loc: Abu Dhabi (Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, opened 2007)
entries.hint: The state appoints imams, standardises the Friday sermon through the General Authority of Islamic Affairs and Endowments, and projects an official 'moderate' Islam. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, which holds over 40,000 worshippers, is its architectural expression.
entries.note: the General Authority of Islamic Affairs and Endowments (Awqaf); the Grand Mosque opened for Eid al-Adha 2007.
keywords: Abu Dhabi Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque

entries.label: The proscription of political Islam
entries.hint: After 2011 the UAE moved decisively against the local Muslim Brotherhood affiliate al-Islah — the UAE94 trial in 2013, the designation of the Brotherhood as a terrorist organisation in 2014, and a sustained regional campaign against Islamist movements.
entries.note: the 2013 UAE94 verdicts; the November 2014 terrorist-organisations list (which also named unrelated Western groups, drawing criticism); Freer, 'Rentier Islamism' (2018).

entries.label: Interfaith infrastructure as statecraft
entries.hint: The UAE created a Ministry of Tolerance (2016), hosted Pope Francis and the 'Document on Human Fraternity' co-signed with al-Azhar (2019), and opened the Abrahamic Family House — a mosque, church and synagogue on one site — in 2023, followed by a large Hindu temple in 2024.
entries.note: the February 2019 papal visit and the Human Fraternity document; the Abrahamic Family House (2023); the BAPS Hindu Mandir, Abu Mureikha (2024).
keywords: Abu Dhabi the Abrahamic Family House

entries.label: The faiths of the majority population
entries.loc: Jebel Ali, Abu Dhabi (Mussafah), Dubai (Oud Metha)
entries.hint: With roughly nine in ten residents non-citizen, the UAE hosts large Christian, Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist communities worshipping in designated compounds and, increasingly, purpose-built churches and temples on land granted by the rulers.
entries.note: the Jebel Ali and Mussafah worship compounds; St Joseph's Cathedral (Abu Dhabi) and St Mary's (Dubai); estimates that Muslims are a minority of the resident population (Pew; UAE census categories).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Burj Khalifa and the Palm, Louvre Abu Dhabi and the Sharjah Biennial

entries.label: The Dubai skyline — Burj Al Arab, the Palm, Burj Khalifa
entries.hint: The sail-shaped Burj Al Arab (1999), the Palm Jumeirah reclaimed island (from 2001) and the 828-metre Burj Khalifa (2010, still the world's tallest building) turned Dubai's skyline into a globally recognised brand and a template other Gulf cities copied.
entries.note: Burj Khalifa, opened January 2010 (SOM / Adrian Smith); Nakheel's Palm Jumeirah; the branding studied in Davidson (2008) and Kanna, 'Dubai: The City as Corporation' (2011).

entries.label: Louvre Abu Dhabi and the Saadiyat cultural district
entries.hint: Louvre Abu Dhabi, opened in 2017 under a 30-year agreement with France for the name and loans, anchors a museum quarter that also includes the Zayed National Museum and a planned Guggenheim. Abu Dhabi's cultural strategy is to buy world institutions rather than only build spectacle.
entries.note: the 2007 France–UAE intergovernmental agreement; Louvre Abu Dhabi (Jean Nouvel), opened November 2017.

entries.label: Sharjah's heritage-and-art strategy
entries.hint: Under Sultan al-Qasimi, Sharjah chose a different path from Dubai — restoring the old town, founding a network of museums, and running the Sharjah Biennial (from 1993), which became one of the more critically respected contemporary-art events in the region.
entries.note: UNESCO 'Cultural Capital of the Arab World' 1998; the Sharjah Art Foundation and Biennial; Sharjah's museum system.

entries.label: Emirati art, film and the Venice pavilion
entries.hint: A small conceptual-art scene around Hassan Sharif and 'the Five' from the 1980s grew into a national pavilion at the Venice Biennale (from 2009), a contemporary art market (Art Dubai, from 2007), and a fitful local film industry — the Dubai and Abu Dhabi festivals ran 2007–2018 before both were closed.
entries.note: Hassan Sharif and the Emirates Fine Arts Society; the UAE National Pavilion, Venice Biennale (2009– ); the closure of the Dubai and Abu Dhabi film festivals (2018).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Branch-campus universities, a Mars probe and a national bet on artificial intelligence

entries.label: The imported-university model
entries.hint: Paris-Sorbonne (2006) and NYU (2010) opened full campuses in Abu Dhabi; Khalifa University absorbed the Masdar Institute; and in 2019 the emirate founded the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, billed as the first graduate-only AI university. The strategy buys research capacity rather than growing it.
entries.note: NYU Abu Dhabi (opened 2010); MBZUAI (announced 2019, first intake 2021); the branch-campus critique (Kanna 2011; academic-freedom concerns raised by scholars barred entry).
keywords: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

entries.label: The Emirates Mars Mission
entries.hint: The 'Hope' probe entered Mars orbit in February 2021, making the UAE the fifth space agency to reach the planet and the first Arab state to do so. It was built by Emirati engineers working with the University of Colorado, part of a deliberate use of space as a national capability-building project.
entries.note: Emirates Mars Mission / Hope Probe, Mars orbit insertion 9 February 2021; the Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre; the LASP (Colorado) partnership.

entries.label: The astronaut programme
entries.hint: Hazza al-Mansouri flew an eight-day mission to the ISS in 2019; Sultan al-Neyadi followed in 2023 with a six-month stay and the first spacewalk by an Arab astronaut. The programme is small but has become a fixture of the state's self-image.
entries.note: Hazza al-Mansouri (Soyuz MS-15, September 2019); Sultan al-Neyadi (Crew-6, March–September 2023, EVA April 2023).

entries.label: The AI strategy and G42
entries.hint: The UAE published a National AI Strategy and named the world's first dedicated AI minister in 2017. The Abu Dhabi group G42 and the Technology Innovation Institute's open-source Falcon models followed; a 2024 arrangement with the US governs the UAE's access to advanced chips amid concern over its China ties.
entries.note: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 (2017); Omar Sultan al-Olama as Minister of State for AI (2017); the Falcon models (TII, 2023); the Microsoft–G42 deal and US export controls (2024).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Abu Dhabi's oil and sovereign funds, Dubai's diversification, and the end of the tax-free model

entries.label: Abu Dhabi's oil and the rise of ADNOC
entries.hint: Abu Dhabi holds the great majority of the UAE's oil — among the world's largest reserves — and its national company ADNOC has moved from a sleepy state monopoly to a group that lists subsidiaries on the stock exchange and targets a production capacity of 5 million barrels a day.
entries.note: OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin (UAE reserves and production); ADNOC's partial IPOs from 2017 (Distribution, Drilling, Gas); the 5 mbpd capacity target.

entries.label: The Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth funds
entries.hint: The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (1976), later joined by Mubadala and ADQ, recycles oil revenue into global assets. ADIA is among the largest sovereign funds in the world; independent estimates put the emirate's combined funds above one trillion dollars, though the state publishes no full figure.
entries.note: ADIA (est. 1976); Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute rankings (estimates, not official); Mubadala and ADQ annual reviews.

entries.label: Dubai's diversification and the 2009 debt crisis
entries.hint: Dubai built a non-oil economy on ports (Jebel Ali, 1979; DP World), aviation (Emirates, 1985), tourism, real estate and finance. A 2009 property crash left the holding company Dubai World unable to service debt; Abu Dhabi provided a $20 billion rescue, and the tallest tower was renamed for its president.
entries.note: the November 2009 Dubai World standstill request; the $20bn Abu Dhabi support; IMF Article IV consultations on Dubai's debt overhang.

entries.label: The free-zone model
entries.hint: Starting with the Jebel Ali Free Zone, the UAE created dozens of enclaves offering 100% foreign ownership, no personal tax and streamlined licensing. The model drew multinational regional headquarters and was widely copied across the Middle East and Africa.
entries.note: JAFZA (1985); the proliferation of free zones (media, internet, healthcare, financial); the 2021 change allowing 100% foreign ownership onshore too.

entries.label: The end of the tax-free state
entries.hint: A 5% value-added tax took effect in 2018 and a 9% federal corporate tax in June 2023 — the first broad taxes in the UAE's history, introduced as oil's share of revenue was planned down and the IMF pressed Gulf states to widen their fiscal base.
entries.note: Federal Decree-Law No. 8 of 2017 (VAT, effective 1 January 2018); Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 (corporate tax, effective June 2023).

entries.label: A population that is mostly foreign
entries.hint: The UAE's population rose from under 300,000 in 1971 to roughly 10 million by the 2020s, of whom citizens are commonly estimated at 11–12%. Indians are the largest single group. The economy runs on temporary migrant labour with no route to citizenship.
entries.note: Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre population estimates; the citizen share is an estimate (the government does not publish a precise figure); World Bank migration data.

entries.label: Nuclear, solar and hosting COP28
entries.loc: Barakah (Al Dhafra); the Al Maktoum and Al Dhafra solar parks
entries.hint: The Barakah plant — four Korean-built reactors, first power in 2021 — is the Arab world's first nuclear power station. Record-cheap solar tariffs at the Mohammed bin Rashid and Al Dhafra parks and the hosting of the COP28 climate summit in 2023 sit alongside continued expansion of oil output.
entries.note: Barakah Units 1–4 (first grid connection 2020; all four operational by 2024); the 2 GW Al Dhafra solar plant (2023); COP28, Dubai, November–December 2023.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Reactors, orbiters, desalination at scale and a surveillance state

entries.label: The Barakah nuclear plant
entries.loc: Barakah, Al Dhafra region, Abu Dhabi
entries.hint: Built by a Korean consortium under a 2009 contract, Barakah's four APR-1400 reactors supply, when all running, about a quarter of the UAE's electricity — the country's largest single engineering project and a deliberate acquisition of civil nuclear capability under IAEA safeguards.
entries.note: the 2009 KEPCO contract; Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation; IAEA and the '123 Agreement' with the US (2009) barring domestic enrichment.

entries.label: Desalination and the strategic water reserve
entries.loc: Jebel Ali; Taweelah; the Liwa aquifer
entries.hint: The UAE depends on desalinated seawater for almost all its drinking water, and has shifted from energy-hungry thermal plants toward reverse osmosis and solar-powered desalination. It also pumps treated water into the Liwa aquifer as a buried emergency reserve.
entries.note: the Taweelah reverse-osmosis plant (one of the world's largest, 2022); the Liwa Strategic Water Reserve project (aquifer storage and recovery).

entries.label: The surveillance apparatus
entries.hint: Investigations have documented the UAE's use of the ToTok messaging app as a data-collection tool, the Pegasus spyware against the activist Ahmed Mansoor and others, and 'Project Raven', a US-staffed offensive-hacking unit. Extensive camera networks and facial recognition underpin the 'smart city' programmes.
entries.note: Reuters 'Project Raven' investigation (2019); the New York Times ToTok reporting (2019); Citizen Lab analysis of Pegasus use against Ahmed Mansoor (2016).

entries.label: The compute build-out and Falcon
entries.hint: The Technology Innovation Institute released the open-weight Falcon large language models from 2023; the state-linked group G42 struck partnerships with Microsoft and OpenAI and announced large data-centre and chip projects, subject to a 2024 security arrangement governing US technology access given the UAE's ties to China.
entries.note: Falcon 40B / 180B (TII, 2023); the $1.5bn Microsoft–G42 investment (April 2024) and the accompanying US-brokered conditions; the 'Stargate UAE' data-centre announcement (2025).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Normalisation with Israel, a Look-East pivot, and influence bought with capital and aid

entries.label: The Abraham Accords
entries.hint: The UAE normalised relations with Israel in September 2020 — the first Gulf state to do so — followed by embassies, direct flights, a 2022 free-trade agreement and rapid growth in trade, tourism and defence-technology links. The move realigned the UAE openly with a US-Israel axis against Iran.
entries.note: the Abraham Accords Declaration, 15 September 2020; the UAE–Israel Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (signed 2022, in force 2023).

entries.label: From Zayed's chequebook to MBZ's hard power
entries.hint: Zayed-era diplomacy ran on aid, mediation and staying out of quarrels. After 2011 the UAE built an expeditionary military, intervened in Yemen and Libya, backed the 2013 government change in Egypt, and used economic weight assertively — a shift from soft power to a willingness to project force.
entries.note: Ibish, 'The UAE's Evolving National Security Strategy' (AGSIW, 2017); Roberts, 'Qatar and the UAE' (2023) on the post-2011 turn.

entries.label: The Qatar blockade and the GCC rift
entries.hint: The UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Egypt cut all ties with Qatar in June 2017 over its regional policy and ties to Islamists, closing borders and airspace for three and a half years. The rift was formally ended at the 2021 Al-Ula summit, but UAE–Qatar and UAE–Saudi rivalry persisted.
entries.note: the June 2017 boycott; the January 2021 Al-Ula GCC summit declaration.

entries.label: Multi-alignment — the US, China, India and Russia at once
entries.hint: The UAE hosts US forces at Al Dhafra and Jebel Ali while making China its largest trade partner, signing a 2022 economic-partnership deal with India, keeping open trade and finance channels with Russia after 2022, and joining BRICS in 2024. It presents this balancing as a sovereign choice.
entries.note: US basing (Al Dhafra Air Base; Jebel Ali as the busiest US Navy port of call abroad); the UAE–India CEPA (2022); UAE accession to BRICS (January 2024).

entries.label: A hub for people and capital — and its scrutiny
entries.hint: The UAE draws migrants from some 200 countries and, increasingly, mobile capital — Russian, Indian, African and other wealth attracted by golden visas and light regulation. It was placed on the Financial Action Task Force 'grey list' for money-laundering weaknesses from 2022 to 2024.
entries.note: FATF grey-listing of the UAE (March 2022 – February 2024); the golden visa scheme (from 2019); reporting on post-2022 Russian capital inflows (e.g. the 'Dubai Uncovered' leak, 2022).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The oil shocks, the Iran–Iraq and Gulf wars, 9/11 and the post-2011 realignment

entries.label: The 1973 oil shock funds the federation
entries.hint: The quadrupling of oil prices after the 1973 embargo gave the two-year-old federation a revenue windfall it spent on federal ministries, roads, schools, hospitals and housing — building a functioning state in a single decade.
entries.note: the October 1973 OPEC price rises; the UAE's first development plans; Peck (1986).

entries.label: The Iranian Revolution and the Iran–Iraq War
entries.hint: Revolution in Iran and the eight-year war that followed turned the Gulf into a war zone — the 'tanker war', the reflagging of Kuwaiti ships, mines and missile strikes. Dubai profited as a trans-shipment point to a sanctioned Iran even as Abu Dhabi backed Iraq.
entries.note: the 1980–88 war and the 1984–88 tanker war; the divergence between Abu Dhabi's and Dubai's tilts.

entries.label: 9/11 and its aftermath
entries.hint: Two of the 19 hijackers were Emirati, and money for the plot moved through UAE banks. The UAE responded by tightening financial controls, deepening security cooperation with Washington, and — like its neighbours — bracing for the regional consequences of the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq.
entries.note: the 9/11 Commission Report on the Emirati hijackers and the UAE money trail; the subsequent US–UAE counter-terror finance cooperation.

entries.label: The 2011 uprisings and the counter-revolutionary turn
entries.hint: The Arab uprisings alarmed the UAE, which saw the Muslim Brotherhood's electoral gains as a threat. It backed the 2013 military takeover in Egypt with billions in aid, and made opposition to political Islam the organising principle of its regional policy.
entries.note: UAE (and Saudi) financial support to Egypt after July 2013; Hassan Hassan and others on the UAE's counter-Islamist strategy.

entries.label: The Ukraine war and the non-aligned Gulf
entries.hint: The UAE abstained on key UN votes condemning Russia's 2022 invasion, kept trade and travel open, and saw a surge of Russian money and migrants into Dubai — positioning itself, like India, as a state that trades with all sides of a great-power conflict.
entries.note: UAE abstentions at the UN Security Council and General Assembly (2022); reporting on Russian capital and gold flows through the UAE (2022–2024).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Citizens and the other 88%, migrant labour, women in public life, and the silenced

entries.label: The citizen–expatriate divide
entries.hint: UAE citizens — an estimated 11–12% of residents — receive free education and health care, housing grants, guaranteed public-sector jobs and no income tax, but no elected legislature. The non-citizen majority has none of the benefits and no route to naturalisation, which since 2021 is open only to a small number of selected professionals.
entries.note: the 2021 Cabinet decision allowing limited naturalisation of investors, doctors, scientists and creatives; the citizen-benefit structure ('the rentier bargain'); Davidson (2005).

entries.label: Migrant labour and the limits of reform
entries.loc: construction sites and labour accommodation across the UAE
entries.hint: Low-paid migrant workers, recruited under debt and tied to employers, built the UAE's cities. Reforms — banked wages, a summer midday work-ban, a 2021 labour law — reduced the worst abuses; researchers and the ILO record that wage theft, recruitment debt and restricted mobility persist.
entries.note: ILO and Human Rights Watch reporting; the Saadiyat Island and Expo 2020 labour controversies; the midday break rule (from 2005).

entries.label: Women in public life
entries.hint: Emirati women outnumber men in universities, hold around a third of cabinet posts, and by directive fill half the Federal National Council since 2019; women serve as judges, diplomats, pilots and astronaut candidates. Elements of male guardianship in family law were only removed by the 2020–24 reforms; most domestic workers are women with weaker protections.
entries.note: the 2019 FNC gender-parity directive; UAE Gender Balance Council data; the 2020–2024 personal-status reforms; the domestic-worker law (2017).

entries.label: Dissent and the stateless
entries.hint: Independent politics, unions and unlicensed NGOs do not exist; the UAE94 defendants and the activist Ahmed Mansoor remain imprisoned, several past the end of their sentences under a 2024 retrial. Tens of thousands of stateless 'bidoon' residents, long denied citizenship, were from 2008 offered Comoros passports instead.
entries.note: UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention opinions; the 2024 'UAE84' retrial; the bidoon question and the Comoros 'economic citizenship' scheme (from 2008).
